The Dual Fate of Quinone–Glutathione Reactions

Rabindra Kumar Behera

Abstract:

Iron is an essential transition metal that supports fundamental biological processes, including oxygen transport, mitochondrial respiration, DNA synthesis, and enzymatic catalysis. To prevent iron-mediated oxidative damage, excess intracellular iron is sequestered by ferritin protein cage. The molecular mechanism by which iron is mobilized from ferritin, the primary iron storage protein, under physiological reducing conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that a set of quinones function as efficient electron-transfer mediators to the ferritin mineral core, upon coupling with glutathione (GSH), the major intracellular reducing agent, thereby promoting reductive iron release. Oxygen consumption measurements revealed that these set of quinones undergo rapid GSH-dependent redox cycling, with oxygen utilization paralleling GSH oxidation. Spectral kinetic analysis further identified the formation of a transient intermediate during the quinone&ndashGSH reaction, providing direct spectroscopic evidence for in situ generated transient species. Although quinone&ndashglutathione interaction facilitates ferritin iron release, however the relative extent of quinone mediated Michael adduct formation in presence of GSH poses a question about the dual fate of quinone&ndashglutathione chemistry (reductant/antioxidant vs toxicity). Understanding these processes may provide mechanistic insight into the interplay between glutathione metabolism, quinone based redox chemistry, iron homeostasis, and oxidative stress, with potential implications for ferroptosis and other iron/quinone associated pathologies.
